overview.title: Displaying the test picture and building a multi-output activation model
overview.main_topic: Listing 10.2 (showing the preprocessed cat image with matplotlib, figure 10.1) and listing 10.3 (a Functional API model that maps the original model's input to the outputs of all its Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers)
overview.central_idea: Because a Keras Functional model keeps every layer's symbolic output, you can build a new model that reuses the trained layers and returns any intermediate outputs you choose. Collecting the outputs of all Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers gives an activation model whose prediction for one image is the list of its feature maps.
overview.importance: Listing 10.3 is the key mechanism of section 10.1 and of feature extraction in general: tapping intermediate layers without retraining or rewriting the network. The same pattern is reused for Grad-CAM (p.325).
learning_objectives: Display an image stored as a float batch tensor with matplotlib
Explain how listing 10.3 selects layers by type and collects their outputs
Build a multi-output Keras model from an existing model's input and intermediate outputs
Predict how many outputs the activation model has and their shapes
prerequisites: The reloaded chapter 8 model and its layer list (pp.309–310)
The Keras Functional API and multi-output models (chapter 7)

summary:
First the authors display the test image (**figure 10.1**, a white cat with blue eyes). **Listing 10.2** imports `matplotlib.pyplot`, turns the axes off, and calls `plt.imshow(img_tensor[0].astype("uint8"))`. Indexing `[0]` removes the batch axis added in listing 10.1, giving a (180, 180, 3) array, and casting to `uint8` makes matplotlib treat the 0–255 float values as ordinary 8-bit pixel intensities.

Next comes the core tool of section 10.1: **a Keras model that takes batches of images as input and outputs the activations of all convolution and pooling layers**. **Listing 10.3** loops over `model.layers`. For each layer that is an instance of `layers.Conv2D` or `layers.MaxPooling2D`, it appends `layer.output` (the layer's symbolic output tensor) to `layer_outputs` and saves `layer.name` in `layer_names` for later use as plot titles. Then

```
activation_model = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)
```

creates a new model that shares the trained layers and weights of the original one but returns all of these intermediate outputs, given the model input.

From the summary on pp.309–310, the selected layers are 5 Conv2D and 4 MaxPooling2D layers, so the activation model has **one input and nine outputs**, which p.312 confirms. It is the book's first practical multi-output model.

paragraphs.excerpt: To extract the feature maps you want to look at, you’ll create a Keras
paragraphs.what_it_says: To extract the feature maps, you'll create a Keras model that takes batches of images as input and outputs the activations of all convolution and pooling layers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of modifying the trained model, you wrap its existing layers in a new model whose outputs are intermediate tensors. Calling it on the cat image gives all feature maps in one forward pass.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is how you get inside a trained network in Keras: any intermediate representation can become an output.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Functional models are graphs of layers; `layer.output` is a symbolic tensor in that graph, so any subset of them can define a new model with the same weights.

concepts.name: Multi-output model
concepts.definition: A Keras model that returns several output tensors for one input.
concepts.intuition: Fit probes to several floors of a building at once.
concepts.technical: `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)` with a list of 9 outputs; `predict` returns a list of 9 arrays.
concepts.significance: It lets you read every intermediate activation in one forward pass.
concepts.example: Outputs range from (1, 178, 178, 32) for conv2d_11 to (1, 7, 7, 512) for conv2d_15.
concepts.misconception: That this creates a new, untrained network. It reuses the original layers and their trained weights.

concepts.name: Functional API (feature extraction from intermediate layers)
concepts.definition: Building Keras models as graphs of layers from symbolic inputs to outputs.
concepts.intuition: Since the graph is explicit, you can choose any node as an output.
concepts.technical: `model.input` and `layer.output` are symbolic tensors; any connected input/outputs pair defines a model.
concepts.significance: Makes interpretation and feature extraction easy.
concepts.example: Listing 10.3, and later the Grad-CAM model mapping inputs to the last conv layer's activations (p.325).
concepts.misconception: That you must rewrite the architecture to access hidden layers.

concepts.name: Displaying float images
concepts.definition: Converting an image array to uint8 before showing it with matplotlib.
concepts.intuition: matplotlib expects floats in [0, 1] or integers in [0, 255].
concepts.technical: `img_tensor` holds float32 values in 0–255; `imshow` would clip floats above 1, so `.astype("uint8")` is used; `[0]` drops the batch axis.
concepts.significance: Avoids an all-white or distorted display.
concepts.misconception: That `imshow` can take the (1, 180, 180, 3) batch directly.

code.title: Displaying the test picture
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.axis("off")
plt.imshow(img_tensor[0].astype("uint8"))
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Shows the preprocessed cat image (figure 10.1) without axes.

line_explanations.explanation: `img_tensor[0]` selects the single image from the batch (shape (180, 180, 3)); `.astype("uint8")` converts float32 0–255 values to 8-bit integers so they display correctly.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `img_tensor` (1, 180, 180, 3) float32 from listing 10.1. Output: a displayed image.
code.theory_link: Confirms the image the model will see (resized to 180×180).
pitfalls: Passing the float array directly makes matplotlib clip values above 1.0, giving a nearly white image.
Forgetting `[0]` passes a 4D array, which imshow rejects.

code.title: Instantiating a model that returns layer activations
code.original_code:
from keras import layers
layer_outputs = []
layer_names = []
for layer in model.layers:
    if isinstance(layer, (layers.Conv2D, layers.MaxPooling2D)):
        layer_outputs.append(layer.output)
        layer_names.append(layer.name)
activation_model = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)
code.what_it_does: Collects the symbolic outputs of every Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layer of the reloaded chapter 8 model and builds a new model from the original input to all these outputs.

line_explanations.explanation: Import the layer classes used for the type check.
Empty lists for output tensors and layer names.

Iterate over the model's layers in order and keep only those that are Conv2D or MaxPooling2D (callout: "Extracts the outputs of all Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers and put them in a list"). Input, Rescaling, GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dropout and Dense are skipped.
Append the layer's symbolic output tensor.
Save the layer name, e.g. `conv2d_11`, to label plots later (callout: "Saves the layer names for later").
Create a model that will return these outputs, given the model input (callout). It shares weights with `model`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the trained `model`. Output: `activation_model`, with input shape (None, 180, 180, 3) and nine outputs (shapes from (None, 178, 178, 32) to (None, 7, 7, 512)); plus `layer_names`, a list of nine strings.
code.algorithm: Filter layers by type → gather outputs → build multi-output Functional model.
code.theory_link: Turns the activations defined on p.309 into retrievable tensors; relies on the Functional API's explicit layer graph.

parameters.name: (layers.Conv2D, layers.MaxPooling2D)
parameters.role: Layer types whose activations are visualized.

pitfalls: This works for Functional/Sequential models with defined inputs; a subclassed model with no static graph has no `layer.output` to tap.
`GlobalAveragePooling2D` is not a subclass of `MaxPooling2D`, so it is correctly excluded.
No retraining happens; editing weights of `activation_model` would change `model` too, since they share layers.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: check the outputs (continued in listing 10.4 on p.312)
print(len(layer_outputs))   # 9
for name, out in zip(layer_names, activation_model.outputs):
    print(name, out.shape)

deeper.title: Which nine activations you get
deeper.body:
Applying the filter in listing 10.3 to the summary on pp.309–310 gives these outputs, in order:

1. conv2d_11 (178, 178, 32)
2. max_pooling2d_6 (89, 89, 32)
3. conv2d_12 (87, 87, 64)
4. max_pooling2d_7 (43, 43, 64)
5. conv2d_13 (41, 41, 128)
6. max_pooling2d_8 (20, 20, 128)
7. conv2d_14 (18, 18, 256)
8. max_pooling2d_9 (9, 9, 256)
9. conv2d_15 (7, 7, 512)

That is 1,472 channels in total, each of which can be plotted as a 2D image (figure 10.3 on p.314 does exactly this).

deeper.title: Analogy: tapping a pipeline
deeper.body: Think of the trained model as a water-treatment pipeline. You don't rebuild it to test water quality at each stage; you add sampling taps after each stage. `activation_model` is the same pipeline with taps installed after every convolution and pooling stage: one input, nine samples out.

misconceptions.claim: `activation_model` is a freshly initialized copy that must be trained.
misconceptions.correction: It reuses the original model's layers and trained weights; only the outputs differ.

misconceptions.claim: The activation model returns the final prediction too.
misconceptions.correction: Only Conv2D and MaxPooling2D outputs are collected; the Dense output is not included.
The batch axis must be removed with `[0]`, and the float values cast to uint8.

takeaways: Listing 10.2 shows the test cat (figure 10.1) using img_tensor[0].astype("uint8") to drop the batch axis and get displayable pixels.
Listing 10.3 loops over model.layers and collects layer.output for every Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layer, saving names for plot titles.
keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs) builds a multi-output model that shares the trained weights.
For the chapter 8 ConvNet this gives one input and nine outputs (five conv, four pooling).

questions.question: Why does listing 10.2 use `img_tensor[0].astype("uint8")` instead of `img_tensor`?
questions.answer: `[0]` removes the batch axis to get a (180, 180, 3) image, and casting to uint8 makes the 0–255 float values display as normal pixel intensities.
questions.explanation: img_tensor has shape (1, 180, 180, 3) and dtype float32 (p.310); matplotlib expects a 3D array and clips floats outside [0, 1].

questions.question: How many outputs does `activation_model` have for the chapter 8 ConvNet?
questions.explanation: There are 5 Conv2D and 4 MaxPooling2D layers (pp.309–310), as p.312 confirms. 5 counts only conv layers; 11 would include the head layers; 1 is the original model.

questions.question: Why does `activation_model` not need training?
questions.answer: It is built from the original model's layers, so it shares their trained weights; only the choice of outputs differs.
questions.explanation: In the Functional API, `layer.output` refers to tensors in the existing graph; building a Model from them does not create new layers.

questions.question: What is `layer_names` used for?
options: To rename the layers of the model
To save the layer names for later, e.g. labeling plots
To select which weights to freeze
questions.answer: To save the layer names for later, e.g. labeling plots
questions.explanation: The callout says 'Saves the layer names for later'. The code does not rename, freeze or compile anything.

questions.question: What shape would the last output of `activation_model` have for `img_tensor`?
questions.explanation: From the summary on p.310, with batch size 1.

questions.question: Could you modify listing 10.3 to also return the output of the GlobalAveragePooling2D layer?
questions.answer: Yes: add `layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D` to the isinstance tuple (or append that layer's output separately); the model would then have 10 outputs, the last of shape (None, 512).
questions.explanation: Any layer's symbolic output can be an output of a Functional model.
